claim: The structure of cyclic 3′,5′-adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) was reported in 1958 by Sutherland and Rall.
source: The structure of the first second messenger, cyclic 3′,5′-adenosine monophosphate (cAMP), was reported in 1958 by Sutherland and Rall.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sutherland and Rall, 1958.

claim: cAMP was generated by incubation of a liver extract with adrenaline or glucagon.
source: It was generated by incubation of a liver extract with the first messengers adrenaline or glucagon (Sutherland and Rall, 1958).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sutherland and Rall, 1958.

claim: cAMP is an almost universal second messenger used to translate various extracellular stimuli into a uniform intracellular chemical signal.
source: Since then, cAMP has been demonstrated to be an almost universal second messenger used to translate various extracellular stimuli into a uniform intracellular chemical signal (Dessauer et al., 2017; Ostrom et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dessauer et al., 2017 and Ostrom et al., 2022.

claim: Adenylyl cyclases (ACs) are biosynthetic enzymes for cAMP from ATP.
source: The biosynthetic enzymes for cAMP from ATP, adenylyl cyclases (ACs), have been biochemically investigated in bacteria and eukaryotic cells (Khandelwal and Hamilton, 1971; Linder and Schultz, 2003; Linder and Schultz, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Khandelwal and Hamilton, 1971; Linder and Schultz, 2003; Linder and Schultz, 2008.

claim: The first mammalian AC was sequenced in 1989.
source: Finally in 1989, the first mammalian AC was sequenced (Krupinski et al., 1989).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Krupinski et al., 1989.

claim: Mammalian ACs display two catalytic domains (C1 and C2) which are highly similar in all isoforms.
source: The protein displayed two catalytic domains (C1 and C2) which are highly similar in all isoforms.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about mammalian AC structure.

claim: The two hexahelical membrane anchors (TM1 and TM2) of mammalian ACs are dissimilar and isoform specifically conserved.
source: The two hexahelical membrane anchors (TM1 and TM2) are dissimilar and isoform specifically conserved (Bassler et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bassler et al., 2018.

claim: The hexahelical membrane anchors were proposed to possess a channel or transporter-like function, properties which were never confirmed.
source: The latter were proposed to possess a channel or transporter-like function, properties, which were never confirmed (Krupinski et al., 1989).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Krupinski et al., 1989 and indicates that the proposed function was not confirmed.

claim: The domain architecture of mammalian ACs (TM1–C1–TM2–C2) indicates a pseudoheterodimeric protein composed of two concatenated monomeric bacterial precursor proteins.
source: The domain architecture of mammalian ACs, TM1–C1–TM2–C2, clearly indicated a pseudoheterodimeric protein composed of two concatenated monomeric bacterial precursor proteins (Guo et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Guo et al., 2001.

claim: Nine mammalian membrane-delimited AC isoforms (mACs) with identical domain architectures have been identified by sequencing.
source: To date, sequencing has identified nine mammalian membrane-delimited AC isoforms (mACs) with identical domain architectures (Dessauer et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dessauer et al., 2017.

claim: The catalytic domains of all nine mAC isoforms are conserved and share extensive sequence and structural similarities indicating a similar biosynthetic mechanism.
source: In all nine isoforms the catalytic domains are conserved and share extensive sequence and structural similarities which indicate a similar biosynthetic mechanism (Linder and Schultz, 2003; Linder and Schultz, 2008; Tesmer et al., 1997; Sinha and Sprang, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Linder and Schultz, 2003; Linder and Schultz, 2008; Tesmer et al., 1997; Sinha and Sprang, 2006.

claim: The two membrane domains of mACs differ substantially within each isoform and between all nine mAC isoforms.
source: On the other hand, the associated two membrane domains differ substantially within each isoform and between all nine mAC isoforms (Bassler et al., 2018; Schultz, 2022; Tang and Gilman, 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bassler et al., 2018; Schultz, 2022; Tang and Gilman, 1995.

claim: The membrane domains (TM1 and TM2) of mACs are highly conserved in an isoform-specific manner for about 0.5 billion years of evolution.
source: Bioinformatic studies, however, revealed that the membrane domains, TM1 as well as TM2, are highly conserved in an isoform-specific manner for about 0.5 billion years of evolution (Bassler et al., 2018; Schultz, 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bassler et al., 2018 and Schultz, 2022.

claim: The Gsα subunit of trimeric G proteins activates cAMP formation by the nine mAC isoforms.
source: Extensive studies on the regulation of the nine mAC isoforms revealed that the Gsα subunit of the trimeric G proteins activate cAMP formation.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about mAC regulation.

claim: Gsα is released intracellularly upon stimulation of G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs).
source: Gsα is released intracellularly upon stimulation of G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), i.e., the receptor function for mAC regulation was assigned to the diversity of GPCRs, which presently are most prominent drug targets.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about GPCR signaling.

claim: In 1995 Tang and Gilman reported that Gsα regulation of mammalian mACs does not require the presence of the membrane anchors.
source: In 1995 Tang and Gilman reported that Gsα regulation of mammalian mACs does not require the presence of the membrane anchors.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tang and Gilman, 1995.

claim: A soluble C1–C2 dimer devoid of the membrane domains was fully activated by Gsα.
source: A soluble C1–C2 dimer devoid of the membrane domains was fully activated by Gsα (Tang and Gilman, 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tang and Gilman, 1995.

claim: The theoretical possibility of mACs to be regulated directly, bypassing the GPCRs, was dismissed.
source: The theoretical possibility of mACs to be regulated directly, bypassing the GPCRs, was dismissed (Schuster et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Schuster et al., 2024.

claim: A cyclase-transducing element connects the TM1 and TM2 domains to the attached C1 or C2 catalytic domains.
source: In addition, we identified a cyclase-transducing element that connects the TM1 and TM2 domains to the attached C1 or C2 catalytic domains.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' previous work.

claim: The transducer elements are conserved in a strictly isoform-specific manner.
source: These transducer elements are similarly conserved in a strictly isoform-specific manner (Schultz, 2022; Ziegler, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Schultz, 2022 and Ziegler, 2017.

claim: Cryo-EM structures of mAC holoenzymes revealed that the two membrane domains, TM1 and TM2, collapse into a tight dodecahelical complex resembling membrane receptors.
source: Furthermore, cryo-EM structures of mAC holoenzymes clearly revealed that the two membrane domains, TM1 and TM2, collapse into a tight dodecahelical complex resembling membrane receptors (Qi et al., 2019; Qi et al., 2022; Gu et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Qi et al., 2019; Qi et al., 2022; Gu et al., 2001.

claim: A chimeric model involving the hexahelical quorum-sensing receptor from Vibrio cholerae and the mAC 2 isoform showed that the ligand directly attenuated the Gsα activation of mAC2.
source: Lastly, we created a chimeric model involving the hexahelical quorum-sensing receptor from Vibrio cholerae which has a known aliphatic lipid ligand and the mAC 2 isoform. We observed that the ligand directly affected, i.e., attenuated the Gsα activation of mAC2 (Seth et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Seth et al., 2020.

claim: Aliphatic fatty acids and anandamide are receptor ligands of mAC isoforms 1–7 and 9.
source: We identify aliphatic fatty acids and anandamide as receptor ligands of mAC isoforms 1–7 and 9.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Aliphatic fatty acids and anandamide enhance Gsα-stimulated mAC activities of isoforms 2, 3, 7, and 9.
source: The ligands enhance (mAC isoforms 2, 3, 7, and 9) or attenuate (isoforms 1, 4, 5, and 6) Gsα-stimulated mAC activities in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Aliphatic fatty acids and anandamide attenuate Gsα-stimulated mAC activities of isoforms 1, 4, 5, and 6.
source: The ligands enhance (mAC isoforms 2, 3, 7, and 9) or attenuate (isoforms 1, 4, 5, and 6) Gsα-stimulated mAC activities in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Substitution of the stimulatory membrane receptor of mAC3 by the inhibitory receptor of mAC5 results in a ligand inhibited mAC5–mAC3 chimera.
source: Substitution of the stimulatory membrane receptor of mAC3 by the inhibitory receptor of mAC5 results in a ligand inhibited mAC5–mAC3 chimera.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The membrane domains of mACs represent a new class of membrane receptors.
source: Thus, we discovered a new class of membrane receptors in which two signaling modalities are at a crossing, direct tonic lipid and indirect phasic GPCR–Gsα signaling regulating the biosynthesis of cAMP.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and inference from the results.

claim: Direct tonic lipid signaling and indirect phasic GPCR–Gsα signaling intersect at mACs to regulate cAMP biosynthesis.
source: Thus, we discovered a new class of membrane receptors in which two signaling modalities are at a crossing, direct tonic lipid and indirect phasic GPCR–Gsα signaling regulating the biosynthesis of cAMP.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and inference from the results.

claim: Bovine lung was used as starting material because lipids are important for lung development and function.
source: Here, we used bovine lung as a starting material because lipids are important for lung development and function (Änggård and Samuelsson, 1965; Dautel et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Änggård and Samuelsson, 1965 and Dautel et al., 2017.

claim: Lipids were extracted from a cleared lung homogenate, acidified to pH 1, with dichloromethane/methanol (2:1).
source: Lipids were extracted from a cleared lung homogenate, acidified to pH 1, with dichloromethane/methanol (2:1).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental method used.

claim: Fraction E from vacuum liquid chromatography enhanced mAC3 activity stimulated by 300 nM Gsα fourfold.
source: Fraction E enhanced mAC3 activity stimulated by 300 nM Gsα fourfold, whereas mAC5 activity was unaffected (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Fraction E from vacuum liquid chromatography did not affect mAC5 activity.
source: Fraction E enhanced mAC3 activity stimulated by 300 nM Gsα fourfold, whereas mAC5 activity was unaffected (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Fraction E2 from reversed-phase HPLC enhanced Gsα-stimulated mAC3 fourfold but had no effect on mAC5.
source: The mAC3 enhancing constituents appeared in fraction E2. It enhanced Gsα-stimulated mAC3 fourfold but had no effect on mAC5 (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: GC/MS analysis of fraction E2 identified palmitic, stearic, oleic, and myristic acid.
source: Subsequent GC/MS analysis identified palmitic, stearic, oleic, and myristic acid in E2 (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: 20 µM oleic acid enhanced Gsα-stimulated mAC3 activity threefold with an EC50 of 10.4 µM.
source: 20 µM oleic acid enhanced Gsα-stimulated mAC3 activity threefold (EC50 = 10.4 µM) and 20 µM palmitic acid twofold (EC50 = 6.4 µM), while stearic or myristic acid had no significant effect.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: 20 µM palmitic acid enhanced Gsα-stimulated mAC3 activity twofold with an EC50 of 6.4 µM.
source: 20 µM oleic acid enhanced Gsα-stimulated mAC3 activity threefold (EC50 = 10.4 µM) and 20 µM palmitic acid twofold (EC50 = 6.4 µM), while stearic or myristic acid had no significant effect.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Stearic acid had no significant effect on Gsα-stimulated mAC3 activity.
source: 20 µM oleic acid enhanced Gsα-stimulated mAC3 activity threefold (EC50 = 10.4 µM) and 20 µM palmitic acid twofold (EC50 = 6.4 µM), while stearic or myristic acid had no significant effect.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Myristic acid had no significant effect on Gsα-stimulated mAC3 activity.
source: 20 µM oleic acid enhanced Gsα-stimulated mAC3 activity threefold (EC50 = 10.4 µM) and 20 µM palmitic acid twofold (EC50 = 6.4 µM), while stearic or myristic acid had no significant effect.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: None of the tested fatty acids affected mAC5 activity.
source: None of these fatty acids affected mAC5 activity (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The action of oleic acid on mAC3 was linear for >25 min.
source: The action of oleic acid on mAC3 was linear for >25 min (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The Km of mAC3 for ATP (335 µM) was unaffected by oleic acid.
source: The Km of mAC3 for ATP (335 µM) was unaffected.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Vmax of mAC3 was increased from 0.62 to 1.23 nmol cAMP/mg/min by oleic acid.
source: Vmax was increased from 0.62 to 1.23 nmol cAMP/mg/min (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Oleic acid did not affect the activity of a soluble, Gsα-stimulated construct from mAC1 and 2.
source: Oleic acid did not affect the activity of a soluble, Gsα-stimulated construct formerly used for generating a C1 and C2 catalytic dimer from mAC1 and 2, ruling out spurious detergent effects (Tang and Gilman, 1995; Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6 and a citation to Tang and Gilman, 1995.

claim: The EC50 of Gsα for mAC3 in the absence of oleic acid was 549 nM.
source: For mAC3 the calculated EC50 of Gsα in presence and absence of oleic acid were 549 and 471 nM, respectively (not significant).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The EC50 of Gsα for mAC3 in the presence of 20 µM oleic acid was 471 nM.
source: For mAC3 the calculated EC50 of Gsα in presence and absence of oleic acid were 549 and 471 nM, respectively (not significant).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Over the Gsα concentration range tested with mAC3, the enhancement of cAMP formation by 20 µM oleic acid was uniformly about 3.4-fold.
source: Over the Gsα concentration range tested with mAC3 the enhancement of cAMP formation by 20 µM oleic was uniformly about 3.4-fold (Figure 2, right).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2, right.

claim: Gsα stimulation of mAC5 was not enhanced by oleic acid.
source: In the case of mAC5, Gsα stimulation was not enhanced by oleic acid (Figure 2, center and right).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2, center and right.

claim: Elaidic, cis-vaccenic and linoleic acids were efficient enhancers of Gsα-stimulated mAC3 activity at 20 µM.
source: At 20 µM, elaidic, cis-vaccenic and linoleic acids were efficient enhancers of Gsα-stimulated mAC3 activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Palmitic, palmitoleic, linolenic, eicosa-pentaenoic acids, and oleamide were less efficacious enhancers of Gsα-stimulated mAC3 activity.
source: Palmitic, palmitoleic, linolenic, eicosa-pentaenoic acids, and oleamide were less efficacious; other compounds were inactive (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Oleic acid enhanced cAMP formation in HEK-mAC3 cells 1.5-fold.
source: Addition of oleic acid enhanced cAMP formation in HEK-mAC3 1.5-fold (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Stearic acid was inactive in HEK-mAC3 cells.
source: Stearic acid was inactive.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: cAMP formation in HEK-mAC5 cells was unaffected by oleic acid.
source: Under identical conditions, cAMP formation in HEK-mAC5 cells was unaffected (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The EC50 of oleic acid in HEK293-mAC3 cells was 0.5 µM.
source: The EC50 of oleic acid in HEK293-mAC3 cells was 0.5 µM, i.e., the potency appeared to be increased compared to respective membrane preparations whereas the efficiency was reduced, possibly reflecting the regulatory interplay within the cell.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: 20 µM oleic acid significantly enhanced Gsα-stimulated activities of mAC isoforms 2, 7, and 9.
source: 20 µM oleic acid significantly enhanced Gsα-stimulated activities of isoforms 2, 7, and 9, mAC1 was slightly attenuated, and isoforms 4, 5, 6, and 8 were unaffected (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: 20 µM oleic acid slightly attenuated Gsα-stimulated activity of mAC1.
source: 20 µM oleic acid significantly enhanced Gsα-stimulated activities of isoforms 2, 7, and 9, mAC1 was slightly attenuated, and isoforms 4, 5, 6, and 8 were unaffected (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: 20 µM oleic acid did not affect Gsα-stimulated activities of mAC isoforms 4, 5, 6, and 8.
source: 20 µM oleic acid significantly enhanced Gsα-stimulated activities of isoforms 2, 7, and 9, mAC1 was slightly attenuated, and isoforms 4, 5, 6, and 8 were unaffected (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The EC50 of oleic acid for mAC2, mAC7, and mAC9 were 8.6, 6.7, and 7.8 µM, respectively.
source: The EC50 of oleic acid were 8.6, 6.7, and 7.8 µM, respectively, comparable to that determined for mAC3.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: 20 µM cis-vaccenic acid doubled cAMP formation by mAC2 with an EC50 of 10.6 µM.
source: In the case of mAC2, 20 µM cis-vaccenic acid doubled cAMP formation (EC50 10.6 µM) while other compounds were inactive (Figure 5C and for additional concentration–response curves see Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The EC50 of elaidic acid for mAC7 was 9.7 µM.
source: For mAC7 the EC50 of elaidic was 9.7 µM (concentration–response curve see Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: 20 µM palmitoleic, oleic, elaidic, cis-vaccenic, and linoleic acid enhanced mAC9 activity three- to fourfold.
source: The range of potential ligands for mAC9 was more comprehensive: three- to fourfold enhancement was observed with 20 µM palmitoleic, oleic, elaidic, cis-vaccenic, and linoleic acid.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: 20 µM myristic, palmitic, palmitoleic, linolenic, and arachidonic acid enhanced mAC9 activity 1.5- to 2-fold.
source: With 20 µM myristic, palmitic, palmitoleic, linolenic, and arachidonic acid 1.5- to 2-fold enhancements were observed (Figure 5C and for concentration–response curves see Figure 5—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplements 3 and 4.

claim: mAC isoforms 1 and 4 were significantly attenuated by arachidonic acid.
source: Testing the panel of lipids at 20 µM with mAC isoforms 1, 4, 5, 6, and 8 we found that isoforms 1 and 4 were significantly attenuated by arachidonic acid, and somewhat less by palmitoleic acid.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: mAC isoforms 1 and 4 were somewhat attenuated by palmitoleic acid.
source: Testing the panel of lipids at 20 µM with mAC isoforms 1, 4, 5, 6, and 8 we found that isoforms 1 and 4 were significantly attenuated by arachidonic acid, and somewhat less by palmitoleic acid.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Eicosa-pentaenoic acid had no effect on mAC1 and mAC4 activities.
source: Of note, eicosa-pentaenoic acid which resembles arachidonic acid but for an additional cis-Δ−17 double bond had no effect on mAC activities (Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: The IC50 of arachidonic acid for mAC1 and mAC4 were 23 and 36 µM, respectively.
source: Concentration–response curves for arachidonic acid with 300 nM Gsα-stimulated mAC1 and 4 yielded IC50 of 23 and 36 µM, respectively, i.e., about twofold higher compared to the EC50 of enhancing ligands (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: cAMP formation in HEK-mAC1 cells stimulated by 10 µM isoproterenol was attenuated by arachidonic acid with an IC50 of 250 pM.
source: Surprisingly, cAMP formation in HEK-mAC1 cells stimulated by 10 µM isoproterenol was attenuated by arachidonic acid with high potency (IC50 = 250 pM), i.e., with higher potency compared to data with membranes prepared from the same cell line.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: mAC4 activity in HEK-mAC4 cells was not attenuated by arachidonic acid.
source: In contrast, mAC4 activity examined under identical conditions was not attenuated (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Anandamide attenuated 300 nM Gsα stimulation of mAC5 and 6 with IC50 of 42 and 23 µM, respectively.
source: Indeed, anandamide attenuated 300 nM Gsα stimulation of mAC5 and 6 with IC50 of 42 and 23 µM, respectively, i.e., comparable to the effect of arachidonic acid on mACs 1 and 4, and distinctly less potently than the ligands for mAC 2, 3, 7, and 9 (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Anandamide significantly attenuated Gsα-stimulated mAC1 with an IC50 of 29 µM.
source: In fact, anandamide significantly attenuated Gsα-stimulated mAC1, but distinctly not mAC4 (Figure 7B). The IC50 of anandamide for mAC1 was 29 µM.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Anandamide did not attenuate Gsα-stimulated mAC4.
source: In fact, anandamide significantly attenuated Gsα-stimulated mAC1, but distinctly not mAC4 (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: 100 µM anandamide attenuated cAMP formation by 23% in HEK293-mAC5 cells.
source: 100 µM anandamide attenuated cAMP formation by only 23% in HEK293-mAC5 cells, the effect was significant (p < 0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The mAC5(membr)–AC3(cat) chimera was successfully expressed and inserted into membranes in HEK293 cells.
source: Successful expression and membrane insertion of the chimera in HEK293 cells was demonstrated by specific conjugation to Cy5.5 fluorophore, using the protein ligase Connectase (Figure 9A, left; Fuchs, 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9A, left and a citation to Fuchs, 2023.

claim: cAMP synthesis of the mAC5(membr)–AC3(cat) chimera was stimulated up to 10-fold by addition of 300 nM Gsα.
source: cAMP synthesis of isolated membranes from these cells was stimulated up to 10-fold by addition of 300 nM Gsα, comparable to membranes with recombinant mAC3 or mAC5 proteins (Figure 9B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: mAC activity in the mAC5(membr)–AC3(cat) chimera was not enhanced by oleic acid.
source: mAC activity in the mAC5(membr)–AC3(cat) chimera was not enhanced by oleic acid, i.e., loss of receptor function, but was attenuated by anandamide, i.e., gain of receptor function (Figure 9C, D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9C, D.

claim: mAC activity in the mAC5(membr)–AC3(cat) chimera was attenuated by anandamide.
source: mAC activity in the mAC5(membr)–AC3(cat) chimera was not enhanced by oleic acid, i.e., loss of receptor function, but was attenuated by anandamide, i.e., gain of receptor function (Figure 9C, D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9C, D.

claim: The IC50 of anandamide for the mAC5(membr)–AC3(cat) chimera was 29 µM.
source: The attenuation was comparable to results obtained with mAC5 membranes, i.e., IC50 was 29 µM mAC5(membr)–AC3(cat) (Figure 9E) compared to 42 µM for mAC5.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9E.

claim: The attenuating receptor property of mAC5 was successfully grafted onto the mAC3-catalytic dimer.
source: This means that the attenuating receptor property of mAC5 was successfully grafted onto the mAC3-catalytic dimer.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: cAMP formation in HEK293-mAC5(membr)–AC3(cat) cells primed by 2.5 µM isoproterenol was attenuated by anandamide by 66%.
source: cAMP formation primed by 2.5 µM isoproterenol was attenuated by anandamide in HEK293-mAC5(membr)–AC3(cat) cells by 66%, (Figure 10), i.e., a gain of function which remarkably exceeded the anandamide attenuation in HEK293-mAC5 cells of 23%.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10.

claim: Oleic acid was ineffective in HEK293-mAC5(membr)–AC3(cat) cells.
source: In HEK293-mAC5(membr)–AC3(cat) cells oleic acid was ineffective, i.e., loss of function (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: 20 µM oleic acid enhanced Gsα-stimulated cAMP formation in mouse brain cortical membranes 1.5-fold with an EC50 of 5 μM.
source: In cortical membranes 20 µM oleic acid enhanced Gsα-stimulated cAMP formation 1.5-fold with an EC50 of 5 μM, almost identical to the one determined for mAC2, 3, 7, and 9 (Figure 11).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 11.

claim: mAC isoforms 2, 3, and 9 are predominantly expressed in mouse brain cortex.
source: Lastly, we prepared membranes from mouse brain cortex in which predominantly mAC isoforms 2, 3, and 9 are expressed, isoforms with demonstrated enhancement of Gsα stimulation by oleic acid (Sanabra and Mengod, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sanabra and Mengod, 2011.

claim: The dodecahelical membrane domains of the nine mAC receptors have distinct, conserved isoform-specific sequences for the TM1 and TM2 domains.
source: This conclusion is based on (1) the dodecahelical membrane domains of the nine mAC receptors have distinct, conserved isoform-specific sequences for the TM1 and TM2 domains Schultz, 2022;
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Schultz, 2022.

claim: The mAC receptors have distinct ligand specificities and affinities in the lower micromolar range.
source: (2) the receptors have distinct ligand specificities and affinities in the lower micromolar range;
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Isoform dependently, ligands either enhance or attenuate Gsα-stimulated mAC activities.
source: (3) isoform dependently ligands either enhance or attenuate Gsα-stimulated mAC activities;
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Receptor properties are transferable between isoforms by interchanging membrane domains.
source: (4) receptor properties are transferable between isoforms by interchanging membrane domains;
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Isoproterenol-stimulated formation of cAMP in vivo is affected by addition of extracellular ligands.
source: (5) isoproterenol-stimulated formation of cAMP in vivo is affected by addition of extracellular ligands;
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Gsα-stimulated cAMP formation in mouse cortical membranes is enhanced by oleic acid.
source: (6) Gsα-stimulated cAMP formation in mouse cortical membranes is enhanced by oleic acid.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In mAC3, the equilibrium of two differing ground states favors a Gsα unresponsive state.
source: We suppose that in mAC3 the equilibrium of two differing ground states favors a Gsα unresponsive state and the effector oleic acid concentration dependently shifts this equilibrium to a Gsα responsive state (Seth et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is based on speculation and inference from the experimental data, supported by a citation to Seth et al., 2020.

claim: Oleic acid concentration dependently shifts the equilibrium of mAC3 ground states to a Gsα responsive state.
source: We suppose that in mAC3 the equilibrium of two differing ground states favors a Gsα unresponsive state and the effector oleic acid concentration dependently shifts this equilibrium to a Gsα responsive state (Seth et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is based on speculation and inference from the experimental data, supported by a citation to Seth et al., 2020.

claim: The equilibrium of ground states of mAC5 favors a Gsα responsive state.
source: In contrast, the equilibrium of ground states of mAC5 probably is opposite, i.e., the one accessible to Gsα stimulation predominates and stimulation by Gsα is maximal.
